summary:
Campeche stands under Mexico's national framework for legal gender recognition, which remains unfinished. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states now operate an administrative procedure for recognizing a person's gender in official documents. Campeche's elected congress passed a 2024 reform to the Civil Code creating such a procedure.

That is the operative fact for anyone crossing into the state. Identity documents can be aligned through an administrative route rather than through litigation, which is what determines how a trans traveller is treated at border checks, in police encounters, and in banking and health services where a mismatched passport or ID invites questions. Human Rights Watch warns that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, so the existence of a Campeche procedure does not establish how the procedure works in practice or how officials handle a foreign trans person's documents.

The enforcement gap belongs in the assessment. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

The only transfemicide statute documented among Mexico's states is Mexico City's "Paola Buenrostro law", approved in July 2024, which criminalises transfemicide with up to 70 years' imprisonment and makes Mexico City the second of the 32 states to do so. The statute took its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and it obliges the attorney-general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community.
tangentialFactors:
Violence against trans people in Mexico intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months.

Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation. Human Rights Watch found in "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. The same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.
localsOnly:
Campeche residents can seek legal gender recognition through the administrative procedure created by the 2024 Civil Code reform, without having to litigate. Human Rights Watch called on the states that still lack such procedures to adopt them.

The transfemicide statute is a Mexico City statute. No Campeche equivalent is documented in the sources consulted here.

Partnership recognition is settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.

Residents face the same enforcement problem identified across the country, namely that progressive legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so formal rights are seldom enjoyed in practice.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources consulted do not document the requirements, fees, timelines or documentation demands of Campeche's 2024 administrative recognition procedure, nor whether it is open to non-residents or foreign nationals.

Unresolved: whether Campeche operates a hate-crime enhancement for offences motivated by gender identity, and whether a Campeche anti-discrimination statute exists, is not sourced here.

Unresolved: no Campeche-specific data on violence against trans people, or on enforcement of the state's recognition procedure, appears in the sources consulted.

Unresolved: how Campeche authorities treat a trans person presenting identity documents issued by a foreign state that do not match presentation is not sourced.
